newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. data to steal the show.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. data to steal the show.

text.p: A flurry of U.S. data next week may reveal fresh signs of renewed vigour in the economy, analysts said, but they will not disrupt euphoric financial markets.

Investors will be showered with key U.S. figures -- the employment cost index on Tuesday, GDP on Thursday, and payrolls Friday -- which will likely confirm the current atmosphere of robust growth with no obvious inflation.
"Most of the figures we're expecting are going to fall into the pattern of a new paradigm economy," said Stephen Hannah, chief economist at IBJ International.
"The probability of a surprise is relatively low," said Neil Mackinnon, chief economist at Citibank here.
Attention in the early part of the week will focus almost exclusively on Tuesday's second quarter employment cost index, which economists will search for new clues on inflation.
A slight increase to 0.8 percent growth from the first quarter rise of 0.6 percent is broadly discounted, but investors may not easily digest a leap in genuine wage inflation.
A steep rise would undermine the widely-accepted view that productivity growth is keeping U.S. inflation at bay. But even that shouldn't turn the market bearish, economists said.
Benign wage pressures are likely to reach a combustion point at some stage, they say. But not yet.
"Clearly there is a risk of some pick up in labour cost growth looking further out," said Citibank's Mackinnon.
In currency markets, dollar bulls will embark on any fresh evidence of inflation-free growth to pierce the critical 1.84 resistance against the weakening mark.

"Next week is a critical week for that," said Hannah. "Do we take seriously the German implied threat of intervention or does the market carry on sailing up?" he said, adding a convincing break of 1.8430 would lift the market to the 1.85-1.90 range.

Remarks from Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing about the need for a stable mark and council member Reimut Jochimsen about their new policy of watching the mark during the summer recess have kept the market on guard.
But analysts say the risk for the mark is still to the downside amid perceptions of a broad membership of a single European currency.

"The problem is that everybody knows the Bundesbank itself doesn't really believe in the effectiveness of intervention. So even if it does, it's not going to be more than a token gesture," said Stephen King, chief European economist at HSBC James Capel.
Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan helped buoy markets this week by saying in his Humphrey-Hawkins testimony that inflation would be quite modest in 1997.
But economists said some of Greenspan's more cautious remarks on inflation were being ignored.
"The market is very vulnerable to being caught out there," said Mackinnon, adding that data signalling a snap back in activity could still be a recipe for higher interest rates.
The second quarter real data GDP on Thursday would be subdued, but Wednesday's new home sales for June would point to a buoyant housing market after a decline in mortgage rates, economists said.
The focus will then grind towards Friday's employment data for July. But this too holds few surprises for investors, hung over from this week's rallies in bonds and stocks.
Non-farm payrolls, previously at 217,000, is forecast to come in around 200,000, while unemployment is likely to stay around a low level of five percent.
"This would make the Fed a little bit more confident that the economy has come off the boil in the second quarter going through to the third quarter," said HSBC's King.
But average hourly earnings can be a sticky area. Economists forecast growth of three cents or 0.2 percent a month, but anything like 6-7 cents could be a cause for concern.

The schedule is light elsewhere. Data next week includes UK June consumer credit on Tuesday, where another large rise is expected due to building society windfalls, plus French unemployment on Thursday.
